purpose: A high-efficiency switch-mode power converter that converts one DC voltage into another with 85% to 95% efficiency. Unlike old linear regulators (like the 7805 or the Nano's onboard regulator) that drop voltage by burning off the difference as dangerous heat, switch-mode DC-DC converters use high-frequency inductors and capacitors to step voltage down (Buck), step voltage up (Boost), or maintain a stable voltage from fluctuating batteries without overheating.

whenToUse.scenario: Powering 5V Arduino or Raspberry Pi from 12V or 24V (Car Battery, Solar, Adapter)
whenToUse.why: A standard linear regulator dropping 12V to 5V at 500 mA burns (12V - 5V) × 0.5A = 3.5 Watts of pure heat—it will burn your fingers and shut down in seconds! A Buck converter converts this with 92% efficiency, remaining cool to the touch and consuming less current from your battery.

whenToUse.scenario: Powering 5V or 12V Devices from a Single 3.7V 18650 Lithium Battery
whenToUse.why: A single rechargeable 18650 Li-ion battery supplies only 3.7V, which is too low to run 5V Arduino boards or 12V motors and locks. A Boost converter steps 3.7V up to a stable 5V, 9V, or 12V.

whenToUse.scenario: Battery Voltage Fluctuates Above and Below Your Desired Target (e.g. 4.2V to 3.0V)
whenToUse.why: A lithium battery starts at 4.2V fully charged and drops to 3.0V when empty. If your sensors require a fixed 3.3V, a Buck can only step down and a Boost can only step up. A Buck-Boost (or SEPIC) converter automatically steps down when full and steps up when empty.

whenToUse.scenario: Powering Multiple Servos, Relays, or LED Strips (High Current 3A to 5A)
whenToUse.why: The Arduino Nano's onboard 5V regulator can deliver only ~400 mA before overheating and resetting. Never power servos, motors, or long LED strips from the Arduino 5V pin! Use an external DC-DC Buck converter to supply 3A to 5A directly to the high-power devices.

whenToUse.scenario: Eliminating Audio Noise and Ground Loops in Vehicles
whenToUse.why: In cars or audio projects, digital noise from microcontrollers bleeds into audio amplifiers via shared ground wires. An Isolated DC-DC converter (like B0505S) completely breaks the ground loop magnetically.

basics.title: Buck (Step-Down) vs Boost (Step-Up)
basics.text: Buck = Input voltage is HIGHER than output (e.g. 12V in -> 5V out). Boost = Input voltage is LOWER than output (e.g. 3.7V in -> 5V or 12V out). Remember: You cannot step DOWN with a Boost converter, and you cannot step UP with a Buck converter!

basics.title: Why Linear Regulators Waste So Much Power
basics.text: Linear regulators (7805, AMS1117) act like variable resistors. Power Lost as Heat = (V_in - V_out) × Load Current. At 12V in and 5V out, over 58% of your battery energy is burned as useless heat! DC-DC switch-mode converters chop power at 150 kHz+ into an inductor, achieving 90%+ efficiency.

basics.title: The Blue Multi-Turn Trimmer Gotcha!
basics.text: The #1 beginner frustration with LM2596 and MT3608 modules! Right out of the box, turning the brass screw 1 or 2 turns seems to do nothing. These are 25-turn precision potentiometers: you must turn the screw 10 to 15 FULL turns COUNTER-CLOCKWISE with a multimeter connected before the voltage begins dropping.

basics.title: Common Ground Rule
basics.text: Always connect the DC-DC converter's GND to the Arduino's GND! Standard non-isolated converters have IN- and OUT- connected together internally, creating a shared reference for your digital control signals.

types.name: Step-Down (Buck) Converter
types.heatDissipation: Very low (Runs cool up to 2A without heatsink)
types.looks: PCB with a toroidal or shielded wire-wound inductor, electrolytic capacitors, and a multi-turn trimmer screw.
pros: Supplies high continuous output currents (up to 3A–5A)
cons: Input voltage must be at least 1.5V higher than desired output (dropout voltage)
uses: 24V 3D printer supply down to 5V for Raspberry Pi/OctoPrint

types.name: Step-Up (Boost) Converter
types.looks: Small red or blue board with a square inductor and tiny high-frequency boost IC (e.g. MT3608).
pros: Generates 5V, 9V, or 12V from a single 3.7V lithium cell or two AA batteries
cons: Output current is lower than input current (Conservation of energy: Pin ≈ Pout)
Cannot output less than input voltage
uses: Boosting 5V USB power to 12V for solenoid locks

types.name: Automatic Buck-Boost / SEPIC
types.voltageRelation: V_in can be higher, equal, or lower than V_out
types.looks: Slightly larger PCB with two inductors or dual-winding choke and central control IC.
pros: Rock-solid constant output even as battery drains from 4.2V down to 2.8V
cons: Slightly lower efficiency than a pure buck converter
Slightly higher cost and board size
uses: Solar panel battery charger input stages
Automotive electronics during engine crank dips

popularModules.name: LM2596 Step-Down Module
popularModules.whenToUse: The classic hobbyist power board. Best for converting 12V or 24V power bricks to 5V for Arduino and multi-servo projects.

popularModules.name: MP1584 / Mini-360 Miniature Buck
popularModules.whenToUse: Fingernail-sized module running at 1.5 MHz. Best for miniature drone builds and tight project enclosures.

popularModules.name: MT3608 Step-Up Module
popularModules.whenToUse: The go-to boost converter for 3.7V Li-ion battery projects to produce 5V or 12V.

popularModules.name: XL4015 Heavy-Duty CC/CV Buck
popularModules.whenToUse: Dual trimmers for voltage and current limit. Perfect for lithium battery charging and driving high-power 10W–30W LEDs.

examples.title: Safely Stepping 12V Down to 5V for Arduino
examples.description: Step-by-step procedure to adjust an LM2596 module with a digital multimeter BEFORE connecting to your expensive Arduino Nano.
